title: Day 1 — Lesson 5: Putting Team Success Above Personal Ego
summary: Confidence is valuable. Unhealthy ego is not. Individual excellence should never become a reason to disrespect colleagues, reject accountability or undermine teamwork.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Humility, cooperation, accountability and shared success

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine two therapists working at Zura Spa.

The first therapist is highly skilled and receives excellent feedback from clients. However, she believes she is better than her colleagues. She refuses corrections, dislikes sharing knowledge and becomes upset when another therapist receives recognition.
The second therapist is equally skilled. She takes pride in her work but also respects her colleagues, shares useful knowledge, accepts feedback and celebrates the achievements of others.
Both therapists may be talented, but their contributions to the team are different.
The first therapist may perform well individually while creating difficulties for the people around her.
The second therapist contributes both through her professional skills and through her willingness to help the team succeed.
True professionalism is not only about how well you perform your duties. It is also about how your behaviour contributes to the success of the people and organisation you work with.
At Zura Spa, individual excellence is important, but it should never become a reason to disrespect colleagues, reject accountability or undermine teamwork.

sections.title: 2. What is personal ego?
paragraphs: Personal ego refers to a person's sense of self-importance, identity and personal worth.
Having confidence, self-respect and pride in your abilities is not wrong.

However, ego becomes a workplace problem when a person's desire to feel superior, always be right, receive recognition or protect their image becomes more important than cooperation and shared success.
Important: Ego is not the same as confidence. An employee can be confident, ambitious and highly competent while remaining humble and cooperative.

sections.title: Examples of ego-driven workplace behaviour
list: Refusing correction because you believe you know everything.
Looking down on colleagues because you have more experience.
Becoming jealous when another employee receives praise.
Refusing to apologise because you do not want to appear weak.
Withholding useful information to maintain an advantage over colleagues.
Insisting on having your way even when a better solution is available.
Taking credit for another person's contribution.
Refusing reasonable assistance because you consider certain tasks beneath you.

sections.title: 3. What does putting team success above personal ego mean?
paragraphs: Putting team success above personal ego means making decisions and behaving in ways that support the team's shared objectives rather than allowing personal pride, rivalry or the need for recognition to interfere with cooperation.
It means understanding that:
list: You do not need to be the most important person in the room.
Another person's success does not reduce your value.
Accepting correction does not make you incompetent.
Helping a colleague does not make you inferior.
Admitting a mistake does not make you weak.
Having more experience does not make you more deserving of respect than others.
Your ideas do not always have to be accepted for you to remain a valuable team member.
sections.closing: Putting the team first does not mean sacrificing your dignity, tolerating mistreatment or allowing others to take advantage of you. It means balancing personal interests with the legitimate needs and goals of the team.

sections.title: 4. Personal ego versus a team-first mindset
table: I must always be right.
I am willing to consider better ideas.
Nobody can correct me.
I can learn and improve.
I am better than my colleagues.
We have different strengths.
Why should I help her?
Can I reasonably assist?
She doesn't deserve the praise.
Her achievement benefits the team.
I cannot admit I was wrong.
I can acknowledge and correct mistakes.
My success is all that matters.
My success contributes to our shared success.
I want everyone to recognise me.
I value both individual and team contributions.

sections.title: 5. Seven ways personal ego can damage teamwork
1. Ego makes communication difficult
paragraphs: An employee who always wants to be right may interrupt colleagues, dismiss suggestions or react defensively during discussions.

Zura example: A receptionist suggests a better way to coordinate appointments, but an experienced therapist rejects the idea without considering it because she believes the receptionist is less knowledgeable.
Lesson: Good ideas can come from anyone, regardless of position or experience.

sections.title: 2. Ego prevents learning and improvement
paragraphs: Employees who believe they already know everything may resist training, correction and new procedures.
Zura example: A therapist refuses to adopt an updated service procedure because she has been practising massage for several years.
Lesson: Experience is valuable, but professional growth requires a willingness to learn.

sections.title: 3. Ego encourages unhealthy competition
paragraphs: Employees may begin viewing colleagues as rivals rather than teammates.
Zura example: A therapist becomes upset when another therapist receives more positive client reviews and begins making negative comments about her.
Lesson: Another employee's achievement should not be treated as a personal defeat.

sections.title: 4. Ego discourages cooperation
paragraphs: Employees may refuse reasonable assistance because they believe certain tasks are beneath them.
Zura example: A therapist refuses to help prepare a treatment room during a busy period, even though she is available, because she considers herself too senior for the task.
Lesson: Professional competence and experience should increase your ability to contribute, not reduce your willingness to cooperate.

sections.title: 5. Ego makes accountability difficult
paragraphs: Some employees may deny mistakes, blame colleagues or make excuses because they want to protect their image.
Zura example: A therapist forgets to prepare supplies for a session but blames the receptionist rather than acknowledging her oversight.
Lesson: Taking responsibility builds credibility. Concealing mistakes damages trust.

sections.title: 6. Ego damages workplace relationships
paragraphs: Constant pride, jealousy, disrespect and refusal to apologise can create resentment between colleagues.
Zura example: Two staff members stop communicating after a disagreement because neither wants to be the first to resolve the issue.
Lesson: Resolving a disagreement is more valuable than protecting unnecessary pride.

sections.title: 7. Ego shifts attention away from shared goals
paragraphs: When employees become more concerned about recognition, superiority or winning arguments, they may lose sight of the organisation's objectives.
Zura example: Two employees argue about who should receive credit for a successful booking while a client is waiting for assistance.
Lesson: Personal recognition should never take priority over essential responsibilities and client service.

sections.title: 6. Confidence, humility and ego: Understanding the difference
paragraphs: These three concepts are often misunderstood.
A good Zura employee should be confident in her abilities, humble enough to learn and mature enough to work with others.

items.label: Confidence
items.body: Believing in your abilities while recognising that you can continue to learn. Example: "I am good at my work, and I am willing to improve."

items.label: Humility
items.body: Recognising your strengths without looking down on others and being willing to learn, acknowledge mistakes and appreciate other people's contributions. Example: "I have experience, but my colleagues also have valuable knowledge."

items.label: Unhealthy ego
items.body: When personal pride or self-importance interferes with good judgment, respect and cooperation. Example: "I am more experienced, so nobody should question me."

sections.title: 7. Practical ways to put team success above ego
A. Learn to accept correction
paragraphs: When someone identifies an area for improvement, listen before responding.
Ask questions if you need clarification.
Avoid automatically interpreting every correction as an attack on your competence.
For example: "Thank you for pointing that out. I understand what needs to improve, and I will work on it."
If you believe a correction is inaccurate, you can respectfully explain your perspective.

sections.title: B. Celebrate your colleagues' achievements
paragraphs: When a colleague receives positive client feedback, recognition or a promotion, congratulate them.
Their success does not make you less valuable.
A workplace where employees celebrate one another encourages motivation and cooperation.

sections.title: C. Be willing to apologise
paragraphs: An apology is not a sign of weakness.
If you speak disrespectfully, make a mistake or inconvenience a colleague, acknowledge it and take appropriate steps to correct the situation.
For example: "I realise that the way I spoke to you earlier was inappropriate. I apologise, and I will handle it better next time."

sections.title: D. Listen to ideas from others
paragraphs: A colleague may have less experience than you but still offer a useful suggestion.
Evaluate ideas based on their value, not merely on who presented them.

sections.title: E. Share knowledge
paragraphs: Do not deliberately withhold useful knowledge because you fear that another employee may become as skilled as you.
Helping colleagues improve can strengthen the entire organisation.

sections.title: F. Give credit where it is due
paragraphs: Recognise the contributions of people who helped achieve a successful outcome.
Do not take credit for work you did not perform.

sections.title: G. Know when to compromise
paragraphs: Not every disagreement needs a winner and a loser.
When several reasonable options exist, be willing to consider solutions that best serve the team's objectives.
However, employees should never compromise professional ethics, client safety or legitimate workplace boundaries simply to avoid disagreement.

sections.title: Case study 1: The experienced therapist
paragraphs: A therapist has worked at Zura Spa longer than most of her colleagues.
A newly employed therapist suggests a more efficient way to arrange treatment supplies.
The experienced therapist responds: "I have been doing this job long before you arrived. You cannot teach me anything."
Expected lesson: Experience should be respected, but it should not become a barrier to learning or collaboration.
list: What attitude is the experienced therapist demonstrating?
How might her response affect the new employee?
What would a confident but humble response look like?
Why should ideas be evaluated on merit rather than seniority?

sections.title: Case study 2: The employee who wants all the credit
paragraphs: Two staff members work together to resolve a difficult booking issue.
One employee later tells management that she handled everything alone.
The other employee feels unappreciated and becomes reluctant to cooperate with her in the future.
Expected lesson: Giving credit fairly strengthens trust and encourages future cooperation.
list: How does taking all the credit affect trust?
Why is recognising contributions important?
How should the employee correct the situation?
What can management do to encourage fair recognition?

sections.title: Case study 3: The colleague who receives praise
paragraphs: A therapist receives excellent feedback from several clients.
Another therapist becomes jealous and begins suggesting that the praised employee is receiving preferential treatment.
There is no evidence supporting the accusation.
Expected lesson: Healthy ambition encourages personal improvement without undermining others.
list: How can jealousy affect team relationships?
What would be a more constructive response?
How can the second therapist use the situation as an opportunity to improve?
Why is another person's success not a threat to your own?

sections.title: 9. Interactive exercise: Ego or team-first mindset?
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 5 Assessment at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: A colleague suggests a better way to organise treatment supplies. Reject the idea because you have more experience / Consider the suggestion and evaluate whether it improves operations / Ignore the suggestion because it did not come from management.

Another therapist receives excellent client feedback. Congratulate her and learn from what she does well / Complain that management does not appreciate you / Tell colleagues that the praise is undeserved.
You make a mistake that causes a delay. Blame the nearest colleague / Keep quiet so nobody discovers it / Acknowledge the mistake and help correct the problem.
A less-experienced employee asks you for guidance. Tell her she should already know / Offer appropriate guidance when you can / Refuse because helping might make her better than you.

You disagree with a supervisor's instruction. Respectfully ask questions and explain any relevant concerns / Refuse to discuss the matter because you feel insulted / Complain to colleagues without seeking clarification.

sections.title: 10. Personal reflection
paragraphs: Every staff member should reflect on the following questions.
These questions are intended to encourage honest self-reflection, not to label employees or embarrass anyone.
list: Do I find it difficult to admit when I am wrong?
Do I become uncomfortable when a colleague receives recognition?
Do I sometimes reject useful suggestions because of who made them?
Am I willing to help colleagues without expecting personal recognition?
Do I treat less-experienced colleagues with the same respect I expect from others?
Can I apologise sincerely when I have behaved inappropriately?
Am I more interested in solving problems or proving that I am right?

sections.title: 11. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what it means to put team success above personal ego.
Identify five ways personal ego can negatively affect teamwork.
Explain the difference between confidence, humility and unhealthy ego.
Describe a situation where personal pride could prevent an employee from accepting correction.
Why is it important to celebrate the achievements of colleagues?
Identify three practical ways you can demonstrate humility and cooperation at Zura Spa.
What will you do differently when a colleague disagrees with you or suggests a better way of performing a task?

sections.title: 12. Seven-day humility and teamwork challenge
paragraphs: The aim is to turn the lesson into consistent workplace behaviour.
table: Listen to a colleague's suggestion without dismissing it
Recognise and appreciate another employee's contribution
Accept constructive feedback professionally
Share useful knowledge with a colleague
Acknowledge and correct a mistake without blaming others
Offer reasonable assistance without seeking recognition
Reflect on one situation where you prioritised team success over personal pride

sections.title: 13. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, employees should take pride in their skills, achievements and professional growth.
However, individual success should never become a reason to look down on colleagues, resist accountability or undermine cooperation.

The strongest teams are not necessarily made up of people who are individually the most talented. They are made up of people who can combine their abilities, respect one another, communicate effectively and work toward common objectives.
A truly valuable employee is not only someone who performs well personally but also someone whose presence helps others perform better.
This completes the five topics under Day 1: Understanding Teamwork and the Zura Team Culture.

remember: You do not become less valuable when someone else succeeds. You do not become weak when you accept correction. You do not lose your importance when you help another person. A great team is built when everyone contributes their strengths without allowing personal pride to stand in the way of shared success.
